The patient is a 19-year-old female, gravida 1 para 0, seen on the hospital antenatal ward for her routine prenatal visit at 28 weeks of gestation. A professional Spanish interpreter was used for the entire visit, and the patient repeated back the key instructions to confirm understanding. She reports good fetal movement, with the baby moving several times a day. She denies vaginal bleeding, leakage of fluid, regular contractions, headache, and visual changes. She has no leg swelling and no burning with urination. Mild evening heartburn is manageable with smaller meals. She takes a prenatal vitamin once daily and has no known drug allergies.

On examination, blood pressure was 112/68 and heart rate 84. Fundal height measured 28 cm, consistent with dates. Fetal heart rate was 144 beats per minute by Doppler. Urine dipstick was negative for protein and glucose. Hemoglobin today was 11.4 g/dL.

Impression is an uncomplicated intrauterine pregnancy at 28 weeks with normal fetal growth and normal blood pressure. She will have the one-hour glucose challenge test today and will receive the Tdap vaccine. Rh immune globulin is not needed because she is Rh positive. Continue the prenatal vitamin once daily. I counseled her on fetal kick counts and the warning signs of preterm labor, and she will return in 2 weeks for her next prenatal visit.
summary: A 19-year-old pregnant woman, gravida 1 para 0, attended a routine prenatal visit at 28 weeks of gestation on the hospital antenatal ward with a professional Spanish interpreter. She reported good fetal movement and denied vaginal bleeding, leakage of fluid, regular contractions, headache, and visual changes. Blood pressure, fundal height, fetal heart rate, urine dipstick, and hemoglobin were reassuring. The assessment was an uncomplicated pregnancy with normal fetal growth. The plan included a glucose challenge test, the Tdap vaccine, a continued prenatal vitamin, kick count counseling, and a return visit in 2 weeks.

note:
Gastroenterology clinic dictation. This is a 74-year-old male seen in follow-up for persistently elevated liver enzymes in the setting of known fatty liver disease. He was referred by his primary care physician after routine labs about three months ago showed elevated transaminases, and a repeat panel last month was still abnormal. His history includes type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, and osteoarthritis of both knees. He is a current smoker, about ten cigarettes a day for many years, and he says he drinks one beer on weekend days, correction, he says two beers on weekend days, so roughly four beers a week. He denies abdominal pain, jaundice, itching, abdominal swelling, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, confusion, fever, and unintentional weight loss. He does report some fatigue and says he has gained about ten pounds over the past year.

Medications as he reports them are metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, correction, lisinopril 20 mg daily, I just looked at the pill bottle he brought, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, and naproxen 220 mg as needed for his knee pain, which he takes most days. No known drug allergies.

On exam today blood pressure 138/78, heart rate 76, temperature 98.2 F, weight 224 pounds, BMI 33. He is comfortable and in no distress. No scleral icterus, no jaundice, no spider angiomata, no palmar erythema. Abdomen is obese, soft, nontender, nondistended, no palpable hepatosplenomegaly, no ascites, no shifting dullness. No asterixis. No peripheral edema.

Data review. Labs from last month show ALT 87, correction, ALT 78, AST 52, alkaline phosphatase 98, total bilirubin 0.8, albumin 4.1, platelets 205, INR 1.0, creatinine 1.1, and hemoglobin A1c 7.6 percent. LDL cholesterol 118. Hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis C antibody negative, ANA negative, ferritin and iron saturation within normal limits. FIB-4 calculates to 2.1, which is indeterminate. Abdominal ultrasound from last month showed diffusely increased hepatic echogenicity consistent with hepatic steatosis, normal liver contour, no focal lesion, no ascites, and a normal spleen size. FibroScan today showed a liver stiffness of 9.8 kPa with CAP 312, consistent with significant steatosis and possible stage 2 fibrosis.

Impression. Number one, elevated liver enzymes due to metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease, with possible stage 2 fibrosis, in the setting of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and ongoing moderate alcohol use which may be contributing. Number two, current tobacco use. Number three, chronic naproxen use, which I am not comfortable with given his liver and his kidney function.

Plan. I am stopping the naproxen today and he can use acetaminophen up to 2 grams per day for the knee pain. I am increasing the atorvastatin from 20 mg to 40 mg nightly, which is safe in fatty liver and will help the LDL. Continue metformin, lisinopril, amlodipine, and aspirin as they are. I advised him to cut alcohol out completely. Start nicotine patch 14 mg daily and I offered a referral to the tobacco quitting program, which he accepted. Referral to the dietitian for a weight loss program, with a goal of losing 7 to 10 percent of his body weight, and 150 minutes of walking a week. I will message his primary care physician about adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist for diabetes and weight. Repeat hepatic function panel in 3 months, repeat FibroScan in 12 months, and hepatitis A and B vaccination status to be checked. Return to clinic in 3 months. End of dictation.
summary: A 74-year-old male with fatty liver disease, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea was seen for persistently elevated liver enzymes. He is a current smoker, drinks about four beers a week, and denies abdominal pain, jaundice, abdominal swelling, and confusion. ALT was 78 and AST 52, ultrasound showed hepatic steatosis, and FibroScan measured 9.8 kPa. Impression was metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease with possible stage 2 fibrosis, tobacco use, and chronic naproxen use. Naproxen was stopped, atorvastatin was increased to 40 mg nightly, a nicotine patch was started, and dietitian and tobacco cessation referrals were made.

note:
The patient is a 44-year-old male seen on the hospital ward on hospital day 2 after admission for observation of severe abdominal cramping with frequent watery stools. He reports a long history of loose stools, about four to five per day, with cramping that improves after a bowel movement and bloating that comes and goes. Symptoms are worse with stress and after large meals. He denies blood in the stool, fever, nocturnal diarrhea, and unintentional weight loss. He has no family history of colon cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. His home medication is loperamide 2 mg as needed, which helps only partly.

Vitals this morning were blood pressure 126/78, heart rate 74, and temperature 98.4 F. The abdomen was soft with mild diffuse tenderness and no guarding, rebound, or distension. Stool culture and Clostridioides difficile testing were negative. Fecal calprotectin was normal, celiac serology was negative, and CRP was normal. Hemoglobin was 14.6 g/dL and white blood cell count was 7.2.

Impression is irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea meeting Rome IV criteria, with no alarm features. The plan is to start dicyclomine 10 mg three times daily before meals and to continue loperamide 2 mg as needed, not to exceed 8 mg a day. He will be referred to a dietitian for a low FODMAP diet trial, and I advised him to keep a symptom and food diary. Colonoscopy is not indicated at this time given his normal inflammatory markers and the absence of alarm features. He can be discharged today and will follow up in the gastroenterology clinic in 4 weeks.

He denied blood in the stool, fever, nocturnal diarrhea, and unintentional weight loss. Stool studies, fecal calprotectin, celiac serology, and CRP were normal or negative. The impression was irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea without alarm features. Dicyclomine was started, loperamide was continued as needed, a dietitian referral was made, and he was to be discharged with follow-up in 4 weeks.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I have here a 6-year-old male who is coming in for his chronic sinus problems. Tell me what has been going on.
Family member: He has had a stuffy nose and a runny nose for almost four months now. It never fully goes away. He snores at night and he coughs a lot when he lies down.
Doctor: Any fevers?
Family member: No fever. No ear pain either.
Doctor: And his eyes? The referral mentioned some eye symptoms.
Family member: Yes, his eyes get itchy and watery, mostly in the morning, and he rubs them a lot.
Patient: They itch a lot.
Doctor: Any swelling around the eyes, or double vision?
Family member: No swelling, and he has not said anything about double vision. His teacher says he sees the board fine.
Doctor: Headaches or face pain?
Family member: No headaches. He does not complain of face pain.
Doctor: What have you tried at home?
Family member: Saline spray sometimes. Diphenhydramine at bedtime, which makes him groggy the next day. Nothing else.
Doctor: Okay. Let me look. His temperature is 98.4, heart rate is 92, and he weighs 21 kilograms. His nose has swollen, pale turbinates with clear to thick white mucus. I used the scope in the nose, the flexible nasal endoscopy, and I see thick mucus draining from the middle meatus but no polyps and no pus. The tonsils are small. His eye exam shows normal eye movements, normal vision on the chart, mild redness of the conjunctivae, and no swelling of the eyelids.
Family member: So what is it?
Doctor: This is chronic rhinosinusitis, most likely driven by allergic rhinitis, and the itchy watery eyes are allergic conjunctivitis. There are no signs of a sinus infection spreading to the eye. I want to stop the diphenhydramine and start cetirizine 5 mg once daily instead. I am also starting fluticasone nasal spray, one spray in each nostril once daily, and saline nasal rinses twice a day.
Family member: How long until it helps?
Doctor: Give it two to four weeks. We will also arrange allergy testing. Come back in 6 weeks, and sooner if he gets a fever, swelling around the eye, or changes in his vision.
Family member: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 6-year-old male was seen with his family member for almost four months of stuffy nose, runny nose, snoring, cough, and itchy watery eyes. There was no fever, ear pain, headache, face pain, eye swelling, or double vision. Examination and flexible nasal endoscopy showed swollen pale turbinates and thick mucus without polyps or pus, with mild conjunctival redness. The diagnoses were chronic rhinosinusitis, allergic rhinitis, and allergic conjunctivitis. Diphenhydramine was stopped, and cetirizine, fluticasone nasal spray, and saline nasal rinses were started, with allergy testing and follow-up in 6 weeks.

soap.subjective: 6-year-old male with almost four months of stuffy nose and runny nose, snoring, and coughing when lying down. Eyes itchy and watery, mostly in the morning. No fever, ear pain, swelling around the eyes, double vision, headaches, or face pain. Has used saline spray occasionally and diphenhydramine at bedtime, which makes him groggy.
soap.objective: Temperature 98.4, heart rate 92, weight 21 kilograms. Swollen pale turbinates with clear to thick white mucus. Flexible nasal endoscopy showed thick mucus draining from the middle meatus, no polyps, no pus. Small tonsils. Eye exam with normal eye movements, normal vision on the chart, mild redness of the conjunctivae, no eyelid swelling.
soap.assessment: Chronic rhinosinusitis, most likely driven by allergic rhinitis, with allergic conjunctivitis. No signs of sinus infection spreading to the eye.
plan: Stop diphenhydramine
Start cetirizine 5 mg once daily
Start fluticasone nasal spray, one spray in each nostril once daily
Start saline nasal rinses twice a day
Arrange allergy testing
Return in 6 weeks, sooner for fever, swelling around the eye, or vision changes

note:
Doctor: Thanks for coming in. I understand you are a 52-year-old female with diabetes, high blood pressure, hypothyroidism, and high cholesterol, on IV antibiotics for a bone infection in your foot, and the home infusion nurse sent you because of loose stools and some soreness at the line. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. I have been getting the ceftriaxone through my PICC line for about three weeks, and for two days now I have had loose stools, like four or five a day.
Doctor: Remind me what the infection was.
Patient: Osteomyelitis in the bone behind my big toe, on the left foot. It came from a diabetic foot ulcer that would not heal. They did an MRI and a bone biopsy, and it grew MSSA.
Doctor: Right. And ceftriaxone 2 grams once a day, planned for six weeks?
Patient: Yes, six weeks total.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever, no chills. No blood in the stool, and no belly pain, just a little cramping.
Doctor: Any redness, swelling or pus at the PICC site, or swelling of the arm?
Patient: The spot is a little sore, but no pus and my arm is not swollen. No rash either, and no shortness of breath.
Doctor: Good. Let's go through what you take. Please include the over-the-counter things.
Patient: Metformin 1000 milligrams twice a day, lisinopril 10 milligrams in the morning, levothyroxine 75 micrograms, and atorvastatin 20 milligrams at night. For supplements I take magnesium oxide 400 milligrams every day for leg cramps, and vitamin D 5000 units daily. Oh wait, the vitamin D is 2000 units, the 5000 was the old bottle.
Doctor: So vitamin D 2000 units daily. How long have you been taking the magnesium?
Patient: About a month, since I started the antibiotic. I read it helps the bones.
Doctor: Okay. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No drug allergies.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 128/76, heart rate 88, temperature 98.9 Fahrenheit, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. The PICC site is mildly tender with no redness, no drainage, and no cord along the vein. The belly is soft and non-tender, with normal bowel sounds. The left foot wound is clean, pink, and smaller than at your last visit. Your labs from this morning show a white count of 8.9, creatinine 1.6, which is up from 1.1 two weeks ago, and an eGFR of 38. The ESR is 62, down from 98. The C. diff test on your stool sample is negative.
Patient: Is the bone infection getting better, then?
Doctor: Yes, the wound and the ESR trend both look better. I think the loose stools are mostly from the magnesium on top of the antibiotic and the metformin. The kidney number is also up, and with the eGFR at 38 the metformin dose is too high.
Patient: So what do I change?
Doctor: Here is my impression. First, osteomyelitis of the left foot from a diabetic foot ulcer, improving on IV ceftriaxone. Second, diarrhea, most likely from the magnesium supplement, and the C. diff test is negative. Third, a mild rise in creatinine, so I am reducing the metformin from 1000 milligrams twice daily to 500 milligrams twice daily. Stop the magnesium oxide today. You can keep the vitamin D. Continue the ceftriaxone 2 grams IV daily through the full six weeks, and keep the lisinopril, levothyroxine, and atorvastatin the same. Drink plenty of fluids.
Patient: Should I stop the lisinopril too, because of the kidneys?
Doctor: Good question. I would keep taking it for now. We will repeat the kidney labs in 3 days with the home infusion nurse, along with the weekly CBC, ESR, and CRP. I will also message your infectious disease clinic about today's visit, and you keep your appointment there next week. If you develop fever, bloody diarrhea, severe belly pain, or redness or swelling at the PICC site or arm, go to the emergency department.
Patient: Okay, I understand. Thank you.
summary: A 52-year-old female with diabetes, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and high cholesterol receiving IV ceftriaxone through a PICC line for MSSA osteomyelitis of the left foot presented with two days of loose stools and mild line-site soreness. She denied fever, chills, blood in the stool, and rash, and she was also taking magnesium oxide and vitamin D supplements. The PICC site and foot wound looked good, the ESR had fallen to 62, creatinine had risen to 1.6 with an eGFR of 38, and the C. diff test was negative. Magnesium oxide was stopped, metformin was reduced to 500 milligrams twice daily, ceftriaxone was continued, and kidney labs were ordered in 3 days.

soap.subjective: 52-year-old female with diabetes, high blood pressure, hypothyroidism, and high cholesterol on IV ceftriaxone through a PICC line for about three weeks for osteomyelitis of the left foot from a diabetic foot ulcer (MSSA). Two days of loose stools, four or five a day, with a little cramping, and some soreness at the PICC site. No fever, chills, blood in the stool, belly pain, pus, arm swelling, rash, or shortness of breath. Takes metformin, lisinopril 10 milligrams, levothyroxine 75 micrograms, atorvastatin 20 milligrams at night, magnesium oxide 400 milligrams daily for leg cramps, and vitamin D 2000 units daily. No drug allergies.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 128/76, heart rate 88, temperature 98.9 Fahrenheit, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. PICC site mildly tender, no redness, drainage, or cord. Abdomen soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. Left foot wound clean, pink, and smaller. White count 8.9, creatinine 1.6 (up from 1.1), eGFR 38, ESR 62 (down from 98). C. diff test on stool negative.
soap.assessment: Osteomyelitis of the left foot from a diabetic foot ulcer, improving on IV ceftriaxone. Diarrhea, most likely from the magnesium supplement, with a negative C. diff test. Mild rise in creatinine.
plan: Reduce metformin from 1000 milligrams twice daily to 500 milligrams twice daily
Stop magnesium oxide; keep vitamin D
Continue ceftriaxone 2 grams IV daily for the full six weeks
Continue lisinopril, levothyroxine, and atorvastatin unchanged
Drink plenty of fluids
Repeat kidney labs in 3 days with the home infusion nurse, plus weekly CBC, ESR, and CRP
Message the infectious disease clinic and keep the appointment next week
Go to the emergency department for fever, bloody diarrhea, severe belly pain, or redness or swelling at the PICC site or arm

note:
Doctor: Hi there. I see you are a 29-year-old female, six weeks after a vaginal delivery, here for your postpartum check. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Pretty good, honestly. Tired, but the baby is a good eater.
Doctor: Are you breastfeeding?
Patient: Yes, exclusively.
Doctor: Any bleeding now?
Patient: No, the bleeding stopped about two weeks ago. No fever, and no pain down there anymore.
Doctor: Any leg swelling, chest pain, or trouble breathing?
Patient: None of those.
Doctor: And how is your mood? Any sadness, anxiety, or trouble bonding with the baby?
Patient: No, I feel happy. I'm just sleepy.
Doctor: Good. Your blood pressure is 114/70 and your heart rate is 72, and your weight is down 20 pounds since delivery. The abdomen is soft, the uterus is back to its normal size, and the perineal tear has healed well. Your breasts are normal with no tenderness or redness. Your depression screening score is 2, which is low.
Patient: Okay. I would like birth control while I am breastfeeding.
Doctor: A progestin-only pill is safe with breastfeeding, so I will start norethindrone 0.35 mg daily today. Keep taking your prenatal vitamin once a day while you nurse. Everything looks like a normal postpartum recovery. I will see you in a year for your annual exam, and call us sooner if the bleeding comes back, you get a fever, or your mood changes.
Patient: Sounds good, thank you.
summary: A 29-year-old female presented six weeks after a vaginal delivery for a postpartum check. She was exclusively breastfeeding, felt tired but happy, and denied bleeding, fever, pain, leg swelling, chest pain, trouble breathing, sadness, and anxiety. Vital signs, examination, and a depression screening score of 2 were normal. The assessment was a normal postpartum recovery. Norethindrone 0.35 mg daily was started for contraception, the prenatal vitamin was continued, and she will return in a year for her annual exam.

soap.subjective: 29-year-old female, six weeks after a vaginal delivery, here for a postpartum check. Exclusively breastfeeding. Feels tired and sleepy but happy. Bleeding stopped about two weeks ago. Denies fever, pain, leg swelling, chest pain, trouble breathing, sadness, anxiety, and trouble bonding with the baby. plan: Start norethindrone 0.35 mg daily for contraception
Continue prenatal vitamin once a day
Annual exam in a year
Call sooner if bleeding returns, fever develops, or mood changes

Doctor: Good afternoon. I have a 19-year-old male here with a C. diff infection that has come back. What has been happening?
Patient: The diarrhea is back. Like five or six watery stools a day for about a week, and I get cramping in my belly.
Doctor: Last time you were treated with vancomycin pills, correct?
Patient: Yeah, about a month ago, after the antibiotics for my tooth infection. I started the vancomycin 125 milligrams four times a day, but the refill was so expensive that I stopped after four days. I could not afford the rest.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. That makes sense, and it is likely why it came back. Any fever, blood in the stool, or vomiting?
Patient: No fever, no blood, and no vomiting.
Doctor: Your vitals today are temperature 98.6, heart rate 82, and blood pressure 118/72. Your belly is soft with mild lower belly tenderness and no distension. Your stool test came back positive for C. diff toxin. The white blood cell count is 11.2 and the creatinine is 0.8.
Patient: So I have to do the antibiotic again?
Doctor: Yes. This is a recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection. I am prescribing fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days, which lowers the chance of another recurrence. Because cost is the problem, our clinic social worker will enroll you in the manufacturer's assistance program today and the pharmacy will confirm your copay before you leave.
Patient: Okay, that helps a lot.
Doctor: Please avoid any antibiotics you do not need, and wash your hands with soap and water, not hand sanitizer. I will see you in 2 weeks, and sooner if the diarrhea worsens or you get a fever.
Patient: Thank you.
summary: A 19-year-old male presented with a recurrence of C. diff diarrhea, with five or six watery stools a day for a week and belly cramping. He had stopped his oral vancomycin after four days a month ago because he could not afford the refill. He denied fever, blood in the stool, and vomiting, and the stool test was positive for C. diff toxin. The diagnosis was recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection. Fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days was prescribed with enrollment in a manufacturer assistance program, and he will return in 2 weeks.

soap.subjective: 19-year-old male with recurrent diarrhea for about a week, five or six watery stools a day with belly cramping. Treated about a month ago with vancomycin 125 milligrams four times a day after antibiotics for a tooth infection, but stopped after four days because he could not afford the refill. Denies fever, blood in the stool, and vomiting.

note:
74-year-old male, f/u visit for MDD med mgmt. Neighbor drove him today (no car, lives far from clinic, bus unreliable). Limited health literacy per pt, prefers verbal instructions, daughter fills pill organizer weekly.

Interval hx:
- On sertraline x 8 wks. Pt states takes 100 mg daily. Bottle reviewed: sertraline 50 mg tab, 1 tab daily. Correction, pt takes 50 mg daily, not 100 mg.
- Still c/o low mood most days, anhedonia, poor sleep (wakes 3-4 am), decreased appetite, low energy. Wt down 4 lb since last visit.
- Takes OTC diphenhydramine 50 mg qhs for sleep.
- Denies SI, HI, hallucinations, mania sx. Denies falls, melena, hematochezia, dizziness. No alcohol use.
PMH: HTN, T2DM, CKD stage 3a, CAD s/p stent, BPH, hyperlipidemia.
Social: lives alone, widowed, daughter calls daily. Independent w/ ADLs, needs help w/ IADLs (shopping, med refills). No firearms at home.
Meds: sertraline 50 mg daily, metformin 500 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, diphenhydramine 50 mg qhs OTC. NKDA.

Vitals: BP 132/76, HR 70, wt 168 lb.
MSE: groomed, cooperative, psychomotor slowing, speech slow but clear, mood "down", affect constricted, thought process linear, no SI/HI, no AVH, oriented x3, insight fair, judgment fair.
PHQ-9: 14 today (was 19 at baseline 8 wks ago). MoCA 25/30.
Labs 1 wk ago: Na 136, K 4.4, Cr 1.3, eGFR 54, TSH 2.3, B12 520, A1c 7.1%.
ECG: NSR, QTc 430 ms.

Dx: MDD, recurrent, partial response to sertraline 50 mg (PHQ-9 19 -> 14), never titrated. Insomnia w/ OTC diphenhydramine use, anticholinergic burden in 74-year-old w/ BPH (Beers list).
- Increase sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg daily (2 x 50 mg tabs every morning). Teach-back done w/ pt, then phone call w/ daughter to update pill organizer.
- D/c diphenhydramine today. Explained why: confusion, urinary retention, falls. Pt verbalized understanding.
- Start mirtazapine 7.5 mg qhs for sleep and appetite.
- Cont metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, tamsulosin, no change.
- Sertraline + aspirin: bleeding risk reviewed, report black stools. Repeat BMP at local lab near home in 2 wks (SIADH risk, age > 65).
- Discussed common side effects (GI upset, low sodium, falls). Pt repeated plan back in own words.
- Large-print med list given, pharmacy to blister-pack all meds, 90-day mail-order refills.
- Transport barrier: next visit by telephone/video in 4 wks, SW referral for medical transport benefit, labs at local lab.
- Crisis line number reviewed. RTC sooner if SI, worsening mood, falls, or black stools.
summary: A 74-year-old male with recurrent major depressive disorder presented for medication management, with limited health literacy and transportation barriers. He had a partial response on sertraline 50 mg after he first misreported taking 100 mg, with a PHQ-9 of 14, and he denied suicidal ideation and hallucinations. He also used over-the-counter diphenhydramine at night, and sodium, TSH, and ECG were acceptable. Sertraline was increased to 100 mg daily, diphenhydramine was stopped, and mirtazapine 7.5 mg at bedtime was started. A sodium recheck, pharmacy blister packs, a telephone visit in 4 weeks, and a social work referral for transport were arranged.

The patient is a 77-year-old female seen in cardiology clinic for follow-up of high LDL cholesterol and statin intolerance, about three weeks after a hospitalization for a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery. She was discharged on atorvastatin 80 mg daily, but she stopped it after about ten days because of severe muscle aches in both thighs and shoulders. She tells me that rosuvastatin 5 mg caused similar myalgias two years ago, which is why she had been on no cholesterol medication before this admission. The myalgias resolved within a week after she stopped atorvastatin. She has no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no palpitations, no lightheadedness, and no bleeding or dark stools while on dual antiplatelet therapy.

Her history also includes hypertension and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes. Current medications are aspirin 81 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, and metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily. She has no known drug allergies.

On examination today, blood pressure was 124/70 and heart rate 62. Weight was stable and there was no leg edema. Heart sounds were regular without murmur, and the lungs were clear. The femoral access site was healed without hematoma. A fasting lipid panel drawn this morning showed total cholesterol 228 mg/dL, LDL 142 mg/dL, HDL 44 mg/dL, and triglycerides 188 mg/dL. ALT and CK were normal, and TSH was 1.8. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm at 60 beats per minute with no acute changes.

Impression is high LDL cholesterol with documented statin intolerance in a patient with a recent non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, and her LDL is well above the goal of less than 55 to 70 mg/dL. I will start ezetimibe 10 mg daily today. Given her very high risk, I will also submit a prior authorization for a PCSK9 inhibitor and start it if her LDL remains above goal at the 6-week lipid recheck. Continue aspirin, clopidogrel, and metoprolol succinate unchanged. A cardiac rehabilitation referral was placed. She will return in 6 weeks with a repeat lipid panel.

Ezetimibe 10 mg daily was started, a PCSK9 inhibitor prior authorization will be submitted, and she will return in 6 weeks with a repeat lipid panel.

note:
Doctor: Hello. I understand you are a 25-year-old female with Graves disease, and you came in today because of a racing heart. Is this your mother with you?
Family member: Yes, I'm her mother. I came along because she has been getting worse for the past two weeks.
Doctor: Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: My heart is pounding all the time, my hands shake, and I'm sweating even when it's cold. I'm so tired, but I can't sleep.
Family member: She has lost weight too, about 12 pounds in a month, and she has been very irritable. I also noticed she ran out of her methimazole about three weeks ago and did not get a refill for a while.
Patient: Yes, I ran out. I was taking 10 milligrams once a day before that.
Doctor: Any chest pain, trouble breathing, vomiting, fever, or confusion?
Patient: No chest pain and no trouble breathing. No vomiting and no fever.
Family member: No confusion either. She is thinking clearly, just anxious.
Doctor: Any sore throat? That matters with this medicine.
Patient: No sore throat.
Doctor: Any eye problems, like double vision or eye pain?
Patient: My eyes feel a bit dry and gritty, but no double vision and no eye pain.
Doctor: Could you be pregnant?
Patient: No, I had my period last week.
Doctor: Okay. Today your heart rate is 118, blood pressure 134/72, temperature 99.1, and respiratory rate 18. You have a fine tremor of the outstretched hands, warm moist skin, and a diffusely enlarged thyroid without nodules. Your reflexes are brisk. Your eyes show mild lid retraction but normal eye movements. The heart is fast but regular and the lungs are clear. The blood work shows a TSH of less than 0.01 and a free T4 of 3.4, which is high. The urine pregnancy test is negative, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia and nothing else.
Family member: Is it dangerous?
Doctor: It is not thyroid storm, because she is alert, her temperature is only slightly up, and there is no vomiting. But it is uncontrolled Graves disease from missing the methimazole. I am restarting methimazole at a higher dose, 20 mg once daily, and starting propranolol 20 mg three times a day to slow the heart and control the tremor.
Patient: Anything I should watch for?
Doctor: Yes. Methimazole can rarely drop the white blood cells, so if you get a fever or sore throat, stop it and call us right away. I am sending a CBC with differential and liver tests today as a baseline. It can also harm a pregnancy, so please use reliable birth control. You will see endocrinology within 1 week, and we will repeat the thyroid labs in 4 weeks. Go to the emergency department for chest pain, fainting, vomiting, or confusion.
Family member: We understand. Thank you.
summary: A 25-year-old female with Graves disease came to urgent care with her mother because of two weeks of a racing heart, tremor, sweating, weight loss, and irritability after running out of methimazole about three weeks earlier. She denied chest pain, trouble breathing, vomiting, fever, confusion, and sore throat. Her heart rate was 118, TSH was suppressed, free T4 was high, and the ECG showed sinus tachycardia. The assessment was uncontrolled Graves disease without thyroid storm. Methimazole was restarted at 20 mg once daily, propranolol was started, baseline blood work was ordered, and endocrinology follow-up was arranged within 1 week.

note:
Reason for consultation: Routine HIV follow-up and review of antiretroviral therapy in a patient with several comorbidities and difficulty attending visits. Requesting service: primary care.

History of present illness: This is a 68-year-old male with HIV infection, diagnosed about twelve years ago according to the referral, correction, about fourteen years ago according to the old records, who is seen in the infectious disease specialty clinic for routine follow-up. He has taken efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate as a single tablet at bedtime since shortly after diagnosis. He reports taking it nearly every night and has missed only one or two doses in the past month, which fits the pharmacy refill record. He lives about 90 miles from the clinic and has no reliable transportation, so he has missed two of his last four visits and relies on a neighbor to drive him. He denies fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, cough, diarrhea, rash, dysuria, and numbness or tingling in his feet. He does report vivid dreams and mild dizziness at night after taking the efavirenz tablet.

Past medical history: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, stage 3a chronic kidney disease, hyperlipidemia, and osteopenia. He has never had an opportunistic infection.

Medications: Metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and calcium carbonate 600 mg daily taken over the counter. He first reported atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, but the pharmacy fill history confirms atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies.

Social history: Retired, lives alone, former smoker who quit 15 years ago, drinks no alcohol, and has no injection drug use.

Physical examination: Blood pressure 148/86, heart rate 78, temperature 98.4 F, weight 82 kg. He is well appearing and in no distress. No oral thrush, no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy, and no rash. Heart sounds are regular without murmur. Lungs are clear. Abdomen is soft and nontender. No peripheral edema. Monofilament sensation is intact in both feet.

Data review: CD4 count 612 cells per cubic millimeter and HIV-1 RNA less than 20 copies per milliliter, and he has been virologically suppressed for more than five years. Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL with eGFR 52. Urine albumin to creatinine ratio 85 mg/g, up from 40 mg/g a year ago. Hemoglobin A1c 7.4 percent, LDL 96, AST and ALT normal, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL. Hepatitis B surface antigen negative with positive surface antibody, hepatitis C antibody negative, and syphilis screen negative. A DEXA scan last year showed osteopenia of the hip.

Impression:
1. HIV infection, virologically suppressed with a CD4 count of 612, on an efavirenz-based regimen. He has stage 3a chronic kidney disease with rising albuminuria on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, osteopenia, and central nervous system side effects from efavirenz, so a switch is appropriate.
2. Hypertension above goal at 148/86.
3. Type 2 diabetes with an A1c of 7.4 percent, stable.
4. Transportation barriers that limit visit attendance.

Recommendations to the primary team:
1. Discontinue the efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate tablet and start bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide one tablet once daily. He should take it with food at the same time as the calcium carbonate, or at least 2 hours before it.
2. Continue metformin 500 mg twice daily. Bictegravir can raise metformin levels, so do not exceed 1000 mg per day and monitor.
3. Increase lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg daily and check a basic metabolic panel in 2 weeks.
4. Continue atorvastatin 40 mg nightly and amlodipine 5 mg daily.
5. Check HIV-1 RNA and creatinine 4 weeks after the switch at a laboratory near his home.
6. Offer the pneumococcal conjugate and recombinant zoster vaccines at his next primary care visit.
7. For transportation, alternate telehealth visits with in-person visits every 6 months, use 90-day mail-order refills, and place a social work referral for the medical transportation benefit.
Thank you for this consultation. We will follow with him.
summary: A 68-year-old male with long-standing HIV infection was seen for routine follow-up, with transportation barriers that have caused missed visits. He denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, and rash, and reported vivid dreams and mild dizziness on efavirenz. He was virologically suppressed with a CD4 count of 612, but had stage 3a chronic kidney disease with rising albuminuria on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, osteopenia, and blood pressure of 148/86. Recommendations were to switch to bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide, increase lisinopril to 20 mg daily, and use telehealth visits, mail-order refills, and a social work referral for transportation.

note:
Emergency department provider dictation. This is a 71-year-old male who presented with sudden onset right flank pain that started about three hours ago and radiates to the groin. The pain is colicky and severe, rated 9 out of 10, and he has had nausea with one episode of vomiting. He noticed pink urine this morning. He denies fever, chills, burning with urination, and chest pain. He has a history of hypertension and a prior kidney stone about ten years ago. He takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies.

Vitals on arrival are blood pressure 154/90, heart rate 96, temperature 98.6 F, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. He is uncomfortable and writhing but nontoxic. Abdomen is soft with mild right costovertebral angle tenderness and no peritoneal signs.

Urinalysis shows moderate blood, no nitrites, and no leukocyte esterase. Creatinine is 1.0 and WBC is 9.4. CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast shows a 5 mm obstructing stone at the right ureterovesical junction with mild right hydronephrosis and no perinephric stranding.

ED course. He received ketorolac 15 mg IV once with improvement in his pain from 9 out of 10 to 3 out of 10. Impression is renal colic from a 5 mm obstructing right ureterovesical junction stone with mild hydronephrosis, no infection, and normal kidney function. A stone of this size has a good chance of passing on its own. Disposition is discharge home with tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily to help the stone pass. He should strain his urine at home, drink plenty of fluids, and follow up with urology in one week. Return to the emergency department for fever, uncontrolled pain, or persistent vomiting.
summary: A 71-year-old male with hypertension and a prior kidney stone presented to the emergency department with three hours of severe right flank pain radiating to the groin, nausea, vomiting, and pink urine. He denied fever, chills, burning with urination, and chest pain. Urinalysis showed blood without infection, creatinine was normal, and CT showed a 5 mm obstructing right ureterovesical junction stone with mild hydronephrosis. The impression was renal colic. He improved with IV ketorolac and was discharged on tamsulosin with urine straining, fluids, and urology follow-up in one week.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I see you are a 56-year-old male with Graves disease, and you are here because your symptoms are getting worse. What is going on?
Patient: I was diagnosed about two months ago. I have been taking methimazole 10 milligrams once a day. But the last couple of weeks my heart has been fluttering, I have lost about 10 pounds, and I feel hot all the time.
Doctor: Any chest pain or shortness of breath?
Patient: No chest pain. A little short of breath when I climb stairs.
Doctor: Any fever, sore throat, or yellowing of the skin?
Patient: No fever, no sore throat, and no yellow skin.
Doctor: Any double vision, eye pain, or bulging of the eyes?
Patient: No double vision and no eye pain. My wife says my eyes look bigger.
Doctor: Do you have high blood pressure or any heart problems?
Patient: High blood pressure, and I take amlodipine 5 milligrams every day. No heart problems.
Doctor: Okay. Your vitals today are heart rate 104, blood pressure 148/82, and temperature 98.7. You have a fine tremor, warm moist skin, and a diffusely enlarged smooth thyroid with a bruit. Your reflexes are brisk. The heart is fast and regular, the lungs are clear, and there is no leg swelling. There is mild lid retraction on the eye exam. The labs today show a TSH under 0.01, a free T4 of 2.9, and a total T3 of 310, all consistent with active Graves disease. The white blood cell count is 6.1 and the liver tests are normal. Your EKG shows sinus tachycardia only.
Patient: So the pill is not working?
Doctor: It is working, but the dose is too low for how high your thyroid hormone level is. I am increasing the methimazole from 10 mg to 20 mg once daily, and starting propranolol 20 mg three times daily for the fluttering and the tremor. The propranolol will also lower your blood pressure a little, so keep taking the amlodipine and we will watch your readings.
Patient: Anything I should watch for?
Doctor: Yes. If you get a fever or a sore throat, stop the methimazole and call us right away, because it can lower your white blood cells. We are also ordering a thyroid uptake scan and will repeat the thyroid labs in 4 weeks. See endocrinology in 2 weeks. Go to the emergency department if you have chest pain, fainting, or a very fast heartbeat that does not settle.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
summary: A 56-year-old male with Graves disease diagnosed two months ago and treated with methimazole 10 mg daily presented with fluttering of the heart, 10 pounds of weight loss, heat intolerance, and mild exertional shortness of breath. He denied chest pain, fever, sore throat, double vision, and eye pain. His heart rate was 104, TSH was suppressed, free T4 and total T3 were high, and the EKG showed sinus tachycardia. Methimazole was increased to 20 mg once daily and propranolol was started, with a thyroid uptake scan, repeat thyroid labs in 4 weeks, and endocrinology follow-up in 2 weeks.

Doctor: Good afternoon. I see you are an 84-year-old female and you came in about a rash. Can you tell me about it?
Patient: Yes. I noticed a red patch on the back of my left thigh about a week ago, and it keeps getting bigger. It feels warm but it does not hurt or itch much.
Doctor: Have you traveled recently?
Patient: I got back about three weeks ago from two weeks in Sweden visiting my sister. We did a lot of walking in the woods near her house. I did not see a tick, but I am sure I got bitten.
Doctor: And I see in your records you were in the hospital after you got back.
Patient: Yes, four days for my heart failure. I had fluid in my lungs. They changed my water pill and sent me home about two weeks ago.
Doctor: Your history lists heart failure, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, and chronic kidney disease. Do you remember the water pill dose?
Patient: Furosemide 80 milligrams once a day. Oh, no, wait, that is wrong, it is 40 milligrams once a day. It used to be 20.
Doctor: Good, so furosemide 40 milligrams once daily since the discharge. What else do you take?
Patient: Lisinopril 10 milligrams in the morning, levothyroxine 50 micrograms, metformin 500 milligrams twice a day, and ibuprofen 200 milligrams when my back hurts. The hospital told me to stop the ibuprofen, but I took a few anyway.
Doctor: Okay, we will come back to that. Any fever, chills, or headache?
Patient: I felt tired and achy and had chills for a few days last week, but no fever today and no headache.
Doctor: Any stiff neck, drooping of the face, joint swelling, chest pain, palpitations, or fainting?
Patient: None of those. No stiff neck, no droopy face, no swollen joints, no chest pain, no palpitations, and I have not fainted.
Doctor: Good. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No, none.
Doctor: Your vitals today are temperature 99.0, blood pressure 118/68, heart rate 78 and regular, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. On the back of your left thigh there is an oval red rash about 12 centimeters across with central clearing. It is warm, not tender, with no blisters or drainage. I see no other skin lesions. Your heart is regular, your lungs are clear with no crackles, and there is trace ankle swelling, unchanged from discharge. Your ECG shows sinus rhythm at 76 per minute with a normal PR interval, so no sign of heart block. Labs today show a white blood cell count of 7.4, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, creatinine 1.1, eGFR 49, and normal liver tests. I sent a Lyme blood test, but it can be negative this early, so I am treating based on the rash.
Patient: So it is Lyme disease?
Doctor: Yes, this is early Lyme disease, erythema migrans, from a tick bite in Sweden. It has not spread to your heart or nerves. I am starting doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days. Take it with food and a full glass of water, stay upright for 30 minutes afterward, and use sun protection because it makes the skin sensitive.
Patient: And the ibuprofen?
Doctor: Stop it completely. With your heart failure and kidneys, it can cause fluid retention and kidney damage. You can take acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for your back instead. Keep taking furosemide 40 mg once daily and the rest of your medications, and keep your heart failure follow-up.
Patient: What should I watch for?
Doctor: Come back or go to the emergency department for fever, severe headache, stiff neck, drooping of the face, palpitations, fainting, or if the rash spreads. I would like to recheck you in one week.
Patient: Thank you.
summary: An 84-year-old female with heart failure, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, and chronic kidney disease presented with an expanding red patch on the left thigh after a recent trip to Sweden and a hospitalization for heart failure about two weeks earlier. She felt tired, achy, and chilled but denied fever today, headache, stiff neck, and chest pain. Examination showed a 12 centimeter oval rash with central clearing, the ECG showed no heart block, and the Lyme blood test was sent. The diagnosis was early Lyme disease with erythema migrans. Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily was started, ibuprofen was stopped in favor of acetaminophen, and follow-up in one week was arranged.
